analysis.one_liner: Bans the Treasury from requiring banks to report customer account deposits and withdrawals to the IRS.
analysis.headline: Backed by 181 Republican cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit the Treasury Department from requiring banks to report the money flowing into and out of customer accounts, beyond the reporting rules already in effect in October 2021. It was written to block a Treasury proposal, floated as part of the Biden administration's tax-enforcement plans, to have banks regularly report account deposit and withdrawal totals to the IRS so it could spot unreported income. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank account holders would be spared any new government requirement that their bank report money flowing in and out of their accounts, beyond the rules already in effect. Banks and credit unions would avoid the expense of collecting and reporting that data. To the extent the blocked proposal would have helped catch unreported income, the largest beneficiaries of its defeat would be people who underreport income, a group concentrated among higher earners and business owners.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers' privacy; banks' compliance budgets

how_it_helps.text: It would forbid the Treasury Secretary from requiring banks and other financial institutions to report the inflows and outflows of customer accounts, except where reporting is already required under rules in effect on October 1, 2021.

That would shield account holders from a proposal to have the government receive regular data on nearly every account's deposits and withdrawals, a plan critics called financial surveillance of ordinary Americans.
It would spare banks and credit unions the cost of building new data-collection and reporting systems for the IRS.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the IRS would lose a proposed new tool for spotting unreported income, and the cost of uncollected taxes would keep falling on wage earners whose income is already reported to the government by employers. Banks would have avoided the cost of building and running new reporting systems.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have blocked a tool aimed at closing the 'tax gap' — the hundreds of billions of dollars in taxes legally owed but never paid each year — leaving honest, wage-earning taxpayers to cover the shortfall through their own taxes.

Unreported income is concentrated among higher earners and business owners whose income is not automatically reported by employers, so blocking the data source protects them far more than ordinary workers, whose wages are already reported on W-2s.

The bill was written as a blanket prohibition with no threshold or safeguards discussion, so it would have ruled out even a narrow version of account-flow reporting designed to catch large-scale evasion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy concern behind the bill was genuine: a requirement that banks regularly report account flows would have created a new stream of financial data about tens of millions of ordinary households headed to the IRS. But the bill drew no lines — it banned the whole category of reporting rather than shaping it with thresholds, carve-outs, or limits on how the data could be used. The cost falls on tax enforcement, and because unreported income skews toward higher earners and businesses, the practical effect of defeating both this bill's death and the underlying proposal is that compliant wage earners continue to shoulder taxes that aggressive filers avoid. A narrower bill with real privacy safeguards would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no markup or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 15, 2021 to prohibit any new Treasury requirement that banks report account inflows and outflows, keeping in place only the rules in effect on October 1, 2021.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, which was the last action ever taken on it.
It drew 181 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic cosponsors.

With Democrats controlling the House and the Financial Services Committee, the bill never received a markup, a floor vote, or any consideration in the Senate before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

Separately, the Treasury proposal the bill targeted — having banks report account flows for tax enforcement — was also dropped from the Democrats' budget reconciliation package, so neither the surveillance proposal nor this prohibition became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks came out ahead: the new reporting and compliance costs they would have faced never arrived (and the underlying Treasury proposal was dropped as well). So did filers with unreported income, since the IRS did not gain the account-flow data that would have helped surface it; ordinary taxpayers' account privacy was also left unchanged.

for.name: Rep. A. Drew Ferguson IV
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar any new Treasury requirement that banks report account inflows and outflows.

for.name: 181 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it one of the larger Republican sponsorship lists of the Congress but no Democratic support.

for.name: Banking industry (including the American Bankers Association)
for.what_they_did: Opposed the underlying Treasury proposal for banks to report account flows to the IRS, lobbying against new account-level reporting requirements.

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a markup or vote on it; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: Support was one-sided: all 181 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on, while the Democratic-controlled Financial Services Committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill would spare banks the cost and work of collecting and reporting account flow data to the IRS. Their interest partly ran alongside customers' privacy concerns and partly against tax enforcement, which banks' resistance to reporting would have weakened.

industries.industry: High-income households and businesses with unreported income
industries.note: The blocked reporting proposal was aimed largely at income that goes unreported to the IRS, which is concentrated among higher earners and business owners rather than wage earners. Killing it preserves the status quo in which compliant wage earners make up the difference.
The IRS would have been barred from receiving any new account-flow data, limiting its ability to detect unreported income beyond existing reporting channels.
